q: Bierzo's 2017 classification ladder ascends village to paraje to viña clasificada to:
exp: Burgundian tiers for Mencía; Raúl Pérez and Descendientes de J. Palacios led.

q: Rías Baixas' five subzones include Val do Salnés, O Rosal and:
ans: Condado do Tea, Soutomaior, Ribeira do Ulla
exp: Salnés is the Atlantic heart; Rosal borders Portugal across the Miño.

q: Which DO ages Palomino under flor unfortified, its 'vinos de pasto' rewriting Andalusian whites?
ans: DO Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, with its sibling DO Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda — since the 2022 revision of the pliego de condiciones, unfortified flor-aged Palomino is legal inside the DO; the vino de pasto pioneers' earlier bottlings had to be sold as VT Cádiz
exp: Equipo Navazos, Luis Pérez, Muchada-Léclapart lead the tide.
Volcanic Canary field blends and braided cordons are exam-favorite exotica.

q: Toro's Tinta de Toro vines survived phylloxera largely because of:
exp: Vega Sicilia's Pintia and Numanthia mine the old vines.

q: Cava's premium tier since 2017, requiring 36 months on the lees and estate discipline, is:
exp: 36 months minimum, single plot, vines 10+ years, max 8,000 kg/ha, estate-vinified, Brut or drier — Gran Reserva is the 30-month tier. Meanwhile Corpinnat seceded entirely — Gramona, Recaredo et al.

q: Which Galician DO terraces Mencía and Godello above the Sil river canyons?
exp: 'Heroic viticulture' — the Romans cut the first terraces.

q: Fondillón, the revived oxidative Monastrell rancio, belongs to which DO?
exp: Overripe Monastrell aged years in old casks — a Renaissance-era name back from the dead.

q: Which Catalan DO holds roughly a third of the world's plantings of Garnacha Blanca?
ans: Terra Alta, the high inland DO in southern Catalunya behind Priorat and Montsant
exp: A high, dry plateau swept by the cierzo, farmed largely through co-operatives, that spent decades selling in bulk and has rebuilt its identity on one variety — garnatxa blanca, which handles the heat, keeps texture rather than acidity, and takes barrel fermentation well. Worth knowing as the answer to 'where does white Grenache actually come from', which candidates usually guess as the southern Rhône.

q: What is a 'Vino de Pago' in Spanish law, and name one.
accept: a single estate denomination such as dominio de valdepusa
estate level do like valdepusa or finca elez
a one-estate appellation valdepusa was the first in 2003
the highest tier granted to an individual estate
ans: The top rung of the Spanish quality pyramid: a single estate with an established name granted its own denomination, which must grow, vinify, age and bottle on site — Dominio de Valdepusa was the first in 2003, with Finca Élez, Guijoso and Pago Florentino among the twenty-odd that followed
exp: It ranks above DOCa in the statute, yet almost every pago sits in an unfashionable region — Castilla-La Mancha above all — because no producer inside Rioja or Ribera del Duero would trade a famous name for a private one. Do not confuse it with Grandes Pagos de España, which is a private members' association with no legal standing. The pair is the cleanest illustration that legal rank and market rank are unrelated.

q: What do VOS and VORS certify in Jerez, and which wines may carry them?
accept: vos is twenty years and vors is thirty for oxidative styles only
20 and 30 years certified for amontillado palo cortado oloroso and px
very old sherry at 20 years very old rare sherry at 30
age certified categories at twenty and thirty years
ans: Minimum average ages verified analytically by the Consejo, carbon dating included: VOS (Vinum Optimum Signatum, 'very old sherry') twenty years, VORS (Vinum Optimum Rare Signatum) thirty years — and only for the oxidative styles, amontillado, palo cortado, oloroso and Pedro Ximénez
exp: No biological wine qualifies: fino and manzanilla live under flor and are refreshed constantly, so age is not the claim they make. Twelve- and fifteen-year categories exist below. And because average age in a solera is a statistical property rather than a fact about any barrel, the Consejo verifies it in the laboratory rather than on paper — one of the few age claims in wine that is actually measured.

q: A red Rioja Gran Reserva must be aged for:
exp: Rioja runs ahead of the national floor. Spanish law asks a red Gran Reserva for 60 months with 18 in cask; Rioja requires 60 months of which at least 24 are in cask and 24 in bottle. Crianza is 24 months with 12 in cask, Reserva 36 months with 12 in cask and 6 in bottle. Note what is being measured: time in a container, not quality, origin or vine age — which is precisely the complaint the 2017 reforms answered with vinos de zona, de municipio and viñedo singular.

q: Trento DOC's founding house and its prestige cuvée:
exp: Giulio Ferrari planted Chardonnay in 1902 after studying in Épernay; mountain traditional method.

q: Franciacorta Riserva demands how many months on lees?

ans: The breakaway association of top Penedès traditional-method growers (Gramona, Recaredo…) who left DO Cava in 2019
exp: Organic estate fruit, 18-month minimum, hand harvest — a protest classification.

q: English sparkling's chalk connects geologically to Champagne via:
ans: The same Cretaceous chalk of the Paris Basin surfacing in the South Downs
exp: Nyetimber (1988 planting) proved it; Taittinger's Domaine Evremond joined in.
